title: TB6-05617
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Nigeria is appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Nigeria is appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection. The Appellant is requesting that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside and substitute the negative determination with a positive determination. The Appellant submits new evidence in support of his appeal and requests an oral hearing under section 110(6) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
This appeal is allowed. Pursuant to section 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, the RAD refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted panel. Background
The Appellant alleges that he is homosexual.

His first homosexual relationship occurred with a boy named XXXX XXXX while they were in secondary school in 2003. Their relationship came to an end when XXXX entered university and the Appellant began to work as a computer operator. The Appellant befriended a customer. Six months later they entered a homosexual relationship which continued until XXXX 2014. In XXXX 2014, the Appellant became friends with XXXX XXXX. They entered a secret homosexual relationship in XXXX 2015. The Appellant and XXXX were together until the Appellant travelled to Canada.
The Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2015 and made a claim for refugee protection on January 12, 2016.

The Appellant had a refugee determination hearing on March 22, 2016. In a written decision issued on April 7, 2016 the RPD rejected the claim. The RPD member found that the Appellant was neither a credible witness nor a homosexual.

Appeal pleadings were received on May 24, 2016. In his appeal, the Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its credibility findings. The Appellant also pleads that the evidence submitted establishes a risk to his life under s. 96 and s. 97(1). ADMISSIBILITY OF NEW EVIDENCE PRESENTED ON APPEAL

As provided for in s. 110(3) of the IRPA, with certain exceptions, the RAD must proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the RPD and may accept documentary evidence and written submissions from the Minister and refugee claimant. Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

The Appellant states in his Memorandum that he submits the following new evidence: a) The original DHL envelope from XXXX XXXX which was made available to the RPD at the hearing part of which is not available to the RAD. b) A notarized Identification card of XXXX XXXX, dated April 21, 2016. c) A notarized Identification card of XXXX XXXX, dated April 22, 2016.

The Appellant submits that the DHL envelope was admitted as evidence at the hearing before the RPD but the signature part of the envelope was not in evidence in the file. The Appellant argues that the RPD sighted (sic) the DHL envelope in paragraph 24 of its reasons and construed it. The RAD assumes that the Appellant perhaps means that the RPD misconstrued the evidence. The RAD notes that in paragraph 24 of the RPD decision, the RPD found that the signature of the sender of the DHL envelope did not match that of the signature on the letter of the sender. The Appellant submits that he could not have envisaged a situation where critical documentary evidence referred to by the RPD would not be before the RAD.

The Appellant argues that documents b) and c) are necessitated because the RPD rejected the Appellant's reasonable and contextual testimony as to why these identification cards had not been notarized when presented as evidence for his hearing.

The RAD finds that it cannot accept document a), the DHL envelope under 110(4) because it is not new evidence. It was evidence presented to the RPD for the Appellant's hearing. The RAD appreciates that the photocopy of DHL envelope made for the RPD file did not capture the sender's signature. The RAD will consider this evidence along with all aspects of the RPD Record in its analysis below.
The RAD does not accept documents b) and c) for the following reasons.

The transcript of the recording of the hearing (the transcript) indicates that the RPD asked the Appellant why the business cards of his former homosexual partners, XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, offered as evidence along with a letter from each man, had not been notarized. The Appellant testified that these were business cards and that is how they were made. The Appellant provided no satisfactory explanation why they were not notarized. The RAD appreciates that the Appellant provided satisfactory explanations as to why the two letters were not notarized. He testified that the authors of the letters feared to let anyone know that they were gay, even a lawyer who might keep such information confidential. However, this explanation does not apply to business cards which contain no information regarding the person's sexual identity.

The RPD's written decision was rendered on April 7, 2016, over two weeks after the hearing. The business card of XXXX XXXX was notarized on April 21, 2016 and the business card of XXXX XXXX was notarized on April 22, 2016. The Appellant provides no explanation as to why the business cards were not made available as post-hearing evidence. Thus, the RAD finds that the Appellant has not established that the evidence was not reasonably available for presentation to the RPD before it rejected the claim.

Even if the RAD were to accept the notarized business cards it would find, as did the RPD, problems with that of XXXX XXXX, which the RAD discusses below. If the RAD were to accept the notarized business card of XXXX XXXX it would find, on materiality, that it is not enough to affect the outcome of this appeal.

The RAD finds that the recent Federal Court of Appeal decision, in Huruglica,1 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal such as the RAD to decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal. [103] I conclude from my statutory analysis that with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law) such as the one involved here, which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard. Thus, after carefully considering the RPD decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the appellant, the RPD erred. Having done this, the RAD is to provide a final determination, either by confirming the RPD decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination of the merits of the refugee claim. It is only when the RAD is of the opinion that it cannot provide such a final determination without hearing the oral evidence presented to the RPD that the matter can be referred back to the RPD for redetermination. No other interpretation of the relevant statutory provisions is reasonable. ANALYSIS OF THE EVIDENCE Did the RPD err in its assessment of the Appellant's credibility? Persecution

The RPD notes in its decision that the Appellant testified that he feared authorities, his family and the Muslim community in Nigeria. The RPD also notes that the Appellant testified that his homosexuality is not known in Nigeria and he was never targeted as a homosexual. The RPD concluded that the Appellant was not part of a persecuted and targeted LGBTQ group in Nigeria.

The Appellant pleads that the RPD misconstrued the evidence he provided. The Appellant submits that information in his Basis of Claim (BOC) form narrative and in his sworn testimony indicated that he was forced to live a secret homosexual life in Nigeria which underscores the persecution that he faced in Nigeria.

The RAD agrees with the Appellant. The RPD erred in its finding. The Appellant's evidence was that he was not able to live openly as a homosexual and he feared serious harm due to his sexual orientation.

Jurisprudence indicates that to be considered persecution, the mistreatment suffered or anticipated [the RAD's emphasis] must be serious.2 One must examine what interest of the Appellant might be harmed and to what extent the subsistence, enjoyment, expression or exercise of that interest might be compromised. The courts have equated the notion of a serious compromising of interest with a key denial of a core human right. In Ward,3 the Supreme Court stated: Underlying the Convention is the international community's commitment to the assurance of basic human rights without discrimination. This is indicated in the preamble to the treaty as follows: CONSIDERING that the Charter of the United Nations and the Universal Declaration of human Rights ... have affirmed the principle that human beings shall enjoy fundamental rights and freedoms without discrimination. This theme ... provides an inherent limit to the cases embraced by the Convention. Hathaway, ... at p. 108, thus explains the impact of this general tone on the treaty on refugee law. The dominant view, however, is that refugee law ought to concern itself with actions which deny human dignity in any key way that the sustained or systemic denial of core human rights is the appropriate standard. Testimony

The RPD found that the Appellant provided either documents that were not credible or no documents to establish his homosexual relationships in Nigeria. The RPD used this basis to find that the Appellant was not credible. The RPD concluded that the Appellant did not have any homosexual relationships in Nigeria and the RPD did not believe that the Appellant had been a homosexual in Nigeria. The RPD found that the Appellant fabricated the story of his sexual orientation.

The Appellant pleads that he testified in a straightforward and spontaneous manner. He argues that his testimony was internally consistent with his BOC form and other evidence he adduced in support of his claim except for one contradiction regarding an application for a visa to the United Kingdom (UK). The Appellant noted that the RPD stated in its reasons that "with regard to credibility, the panel is aware that testimony given under oath is presumed to be true, unless there is valid reason to doubt the truthfulness"4 and then argues further that there is no valid reason adduced by the RPD for it to doubt the truthfulness of his sworn testimony.

The RAD agrees that, other than the Appellant's testimony regarding an application for a visa to the UK there were no obvious contradictions between the Appellant's testimony and information contained in his BOC form.

The RAD also agrees that the RPD's reliance on the lack of documentary evidence for its credibility findings is flawed. The RPD erred in this finding. The RPD in its reasons found no inconsistencies in the Appellant's testimony when compared to information the Appellant provided in his BOC form. The RPD may reasonably draw an adverse credibility inference from an Appellant's failure to present evidence supporting his claim if the account consists of a lack of credibility on key issues, stemming from clear inconsistencies and implausibilities in oral testimony. The RAD is guided by the jurisprudence for the proposition that the RPD is entitled to draw a negative inference from an Appellant's failure to provide corroborating evidence when there are inconsistencies in the claimant's testimony.5 In addition, Justice Martineau held in Morka that in certain circumstances, where the claimant's account lacks credibility on key issues, it is reasonable to ground an adverse credibility finding on an absence of documentation to support an applicant's allegations.6

Regardless of the RPD making no credibility findings regarding the Appellant's testimony the RAD finds that information gathered during the hearing before the RPD is insufficient for the RAD to make its own credibility findings. The RAD is, therefore, unable to conclude that the Appellant is a Convention refugee. The RAD's reasons follow.

According to the transcript there were instances where the RPD provided the Appellant with information contained in his BOC form narrative and then asked the Appellant to confirm the information. For example, the Appellant alleges in his BOC narrative7 that he became friends with XXXX XXXX when they met at school on the soccer field and a homosexual relationship developed. At one point the RPD pointed out to the Appellant that the Appellant was telling him in his narrative that he, the Appellant, had a couple of same sex relationships. The Appellant responded in the affirmation. Shortly after that the RPD stated, "Your basis of claim also indicates in the narrative that there was a guy who was XXXX XXXX." The Appellant responded in the affirmative. The RPD stated "you had a relationship with him" and, again, the Appellant responded in the affirmative. A little later that RPD stated "and you were in secondary school at the time" to which the Appellant responded in the affirmative. The RPD then stated "He played soccer with you". Again, the Appellant responded in the affirmative. The RAD is unable to make credibility findings given that leading questions were put to the Appellant.

The RAD finds that another method of questioning by the RPD was such that the Appellant was required to provide one or two word answers rather than any detail. For example, the RPD asked the Appellant when his relationship with XXXX XXXX began. The Appellant testified that it was in XXXX 2002. The RPD then asked the Appellant how long the relationship lasted. The Appellant testified that the relationship lasted until XXXX 2007. The RPD then asked the Appellant if XXXX XXXX had been in school with him; the Appellant responded in the affirmative. The RAD is unable to determine if the Appellant could be consistent with his story given that the questions put to the Appellant by the RPD followed the Appellant's narrative simplistically and in chronological order.

In his written BOC form narrative the Appellant alleges that he began work as a XXXX XXXX in 2008 and had a homosexual relationship with one of his customers.8 The Appellant provided no precise details about the timeline of this alleged relationship. The RPD did not question the Appellant about this alleged relationship. The Appellant was not asked why he did not provide further detail about the relationship and in particular why he did not provide the name of this alleged homosexual partner.

In his written BOC form narrative, the Appellant alleges that he became friends with XXXX XXXX in XXXX 2014 and they began a secret homosexual relationship in XXXX 2015.9 The RPD did not ask the Appellant why he provided no further details about this relationship in his written narrative. The RPD asked the Appellant few questions about the relationship. The RPD asked if Mr. XXXX was a businessman, to which the Appellant answered in the negative. When asked, the Appellant testified that Mr. XXXX worked in a XXXX. Upon being asked where they met, the Appellant responded that he met Mr. XXXX in XXXX 2014. When the question was repeated, the Appellant testified that they met at a mall. What little testimony the Appellant gave in this regard was consistent with information found in a letter from XXXX XXXX. The RAD has concerns about the lack of information provided in the Appellant's written narrative regarding the alleged homosexual relationship with XXXX XXXX. The RAD also has concerns that information regarding the relationship was provided only in a letter that was written after the Appellant made his claim for refugee protection. Documents provided as evidence by the Appellant

The RPD found that the letter from and business card of XXXX XXXX10 were fabricated to bolster the Appellant's claim for protection. In its reasons, the RPD indicated that the Appellant provided no satisfactory reason why these two documents had not been notarized. The RPD also found that the signature on the business card did not match the signature on the letter. The RPD also found that the signature on the business card did not match the signature on the DHL envelope.
As stated above, the Appellant had concerns about the RPD's findings in this regard.

While the RAD does not agree with the RPD concerning the lack of notarization on the letter from an alleged homosexual in Nigeria, the RAD does agree with the RPD's finding with respect to the signatures. While the RAD is not a handwriting expert, the simplistic signature on the letter from XXXX XXXX is significantly different from the flourish of a signature on the business card. The RAD has examined the original DHL envelope provided by the Appellant in his appeal. The RAD finds that the simplistic signature on the DHL envelope sent by XXXX XXXX differs significantly from the flourish of a signature on the business card.11 The RAD, therefore, assigns no weight to these documents.

The RPD considered the letters provided by the Appellant from two organizations in Toronto that support sexual minorities: XXXX XXXXCentre and XXXX XXXX. The RPD found that these documents are not conclusive about the Appellant's sexual orientation.

The Appellant pleads that the RPD misevaluated the evidence from the XXXX XXXX Centre and XXXX XXXX. The Appellant argues that the letter from XXXX XXXX Centre specifies that he is an active member in the group "Among Friends" a group for LGBT refugee claimants only.

The RAD finds that the letters from the XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX confirm the Appellant's attendance at activities provided by these two organizations. However, simple attendance at either centre does not establish one's sexual identity.
On the basis of the totality of the evidence, the RAD finds that the RPD's overall determination cannot be confirmed.
Since the RAD did not allow new evidence, an oral hearing pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA is not allowed.

Section 111(1) of the IRPA allows the RAD to: (a) confirm the determination of the RPD; (b) set aside a decision of the RPD and substitute a determination that, in its opinion, should have been made; or (c) refer the matter back to the RPD, giving the directions to the RPD that it considers appropriate.

The RAD can make the referral described in section 111(1)(c) only if it was of the opinion that the decision of the RPD was wrong in law, in fact, or in mixed law and fact, and if the RAD cannot make a decision to confirm or substitute the RPD's decision without hearing evidence that was presented to the RPD.12 The Appellant asks the RAD to substitute its own determination that he is a Convention refugee. The RAD is not in a position to do so. The RAD finds that there remain significant credibility concerns which were not addressed by the RPD. The RAD has not seen or questioned the Appellant and is therefore in no position to make its own credibility finding on his refugee claim. Similarly, the RAD is unable to make a finding regarding the Appellant's sexuality. For these reasons, the RAD cannot substitute its own determination for that of the RPD, and it cannot find the Appellant to be a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the Refugee Appeal Division refers the matter to the Refugee Protection Division for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel. This appeal is allowed. (signed) "Lesley Mason" Lesley Mason July 06, 2016 Date 1 M.C.I. v. Huruglica, Bujar (F.C.A., no.
